planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in deep to moderate shade; Petite is the smallest widely sold peace lily selection, staying compact enough for a desk or narrow windowsill without ever needing the repotting a full-size cultivar requires.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in deep to moderate shade, keeping the plant warm above 60°F and away from direct sun and drying drafts. Petite is the miniature end of the peace lily size range, forming a dense, low rosette of narrow, glossy dark green leaves rarely exceeding 12 inches, topped by small white spathe flowers held just above the foliage. Its small mature size makes it the standard choice for terrariums, dish gardens, bathroom shelves, and any spot too tight for a standard peace lily. Like larger peace lily cultivars it wilts dramatically when the soil dries out and rebounds within hours of watering, an easy visual cue that suits forgetful waterers.
sources: NASA Clean Air Study (Wolverton et al., 1989)

planting.note: Divide rhizome tubers and pot in well-drained potting mix; Zamicro is a super-dwarf ZZ selection bred for small containers and tabletop use, staying noticeably shorter and denser than even the compact 'Zenzi' cultivar.

directions: Pot in a well-drained mix over a bed of underground water-storing rhizomes and place in low to bright indirect light. Zamicro is the smallest of the widely marketed ZZ plant selections, producing tightly packed, glossy dark green pinnate leaves on short, upright stems that rarely exceed 10 inches, considerably more compact than both the standard species and the mid-size 'Zenzi' cultivar. Its diminutive scale suits it to small pots, terrariums, and desks where a full-size ZZ plant would quickly outgrow the space, while retaining the same drought tolerance and near-indestructible reputation as its larger relatives. Allow the potting mix to dry out well between waterings, since the water-storing rhizomes rot readily in constantly wet soil.

planting.note: Plant outdoors after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March-May and bring containers indoors before temperatures drop below 35°F in fall. Remove any all-green reversion shoots immediately to keep the cream variegation from being overtaken.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light to partial shade in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix or garden soil. Janine carries irregular cream-white variegation concentrated toward the leaflet margins, a softer, more painterly pattern than the bolder yellow splashes of Trinette or Gold Capella, giving the glossy, umbrella-shaped compound leaves a cooler, frostier overall look. In zone 10-11 it can remain outdoors year-round as a landscape shrub; in zone 9 it is best managed as a container specimen moved outdoors for the warm season and overwintered indoors in bright light. Prune leggy stems in spring to maintain a bushy, compact form, since schefflera responds well to hard pruning.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, moderately fertile, well-drained soil in part shade to bright indirect light. Amate stays noticeably more compact and slower-growing than the species, making it a more manageable choice for interior plantscaping and large containers. CAUTION: invasive in Florida and Hawaii — grow only in containers or as an indoor plant in those states.

directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, well-drained soil in part shade to bright indirect light; CAUTION — invasive in Florida and Hawaii, so grow it only as a contained houseplant in those states rather than in the ground. Amate is a selected, more compact form of umbrella tree bred for interior plantscaping, holding larger, broader, deeper green leaflets on a slower-growing, denser framework than seed-grown Schefflera actinophylla, which makes it easier to manage as a large container specimen indoors or on a shaded patio. It still produces the same bold, palmate compound leaves radiating like umbrella ribs that give the species its common name, just on a scale better suited to interior spaces than the 25- to 40-foot landscape tree the straight species becomes in frost-free zones. Water when the top inch of soil dries and wipe dust from the broad leaflets periodically to keep pores clear; all parts are toxic if ingested.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Invasive Plants

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, fertile potting mix; Tropic Marianne is frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere as an indoor foliage plant.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light — never direct sun — in well-drained, fertile, consistently moist potting mix. Tropic Marianne is a large, vigorous dumb cane cultivar with broad, pale chartreuse-to-cream leaf centers bordered by a wide, dark green margin, a bolder and more saturated color contrast than the narrower cream striping of Camille. Its thick, cane-like stem drops lower leaves as it grows, exposing an attractive trunk beneath an upper crown of foliage, and well-grown specimens make a substantial architectural statement on a shaded porch or in a large interior container. Keep all parts away from children and pets — the sap contains calcium oxalate crystals that cause intense mouth and throat irritation if chewed, the source of the common name 'dumb cane.'
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Dieffenbachia Species for Florida Interiors and Shade Gardens

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, fertile potting mix; Rudolph Roehrs needs brighter indirect light than plain green dieffenbachia cultivars to hold its pale golden coloring well.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, fertile, consistently moist potting mix. Rudolph Roehrs is one of the oldest named dieffenbachia cultivars still in cultivation, prized for leaves that are almost entirely pale chartreuse to yellow-green with only a narrow dark green margin and midrib, a much lighter overall coloring than most speckled or centrally-variegated dumb cane cultivars. That pale coloring means it needs brighter indirect light than deeper-green dieffenbachia to avoid reverting to duller green growth, though it should still be kept out of direct sun, which scorches the thin, chlorophyll-poor leaf tissue. Keep it away from children and pets, since the sap's calcium oxalate crystals cause severe mouth and throat irritation if chewed.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Dieffenbachia Species for Florida Interiors and Shade Gardens

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, fertile potting mix; Sparkles is a compact dieffenbachia cultivar suited to tabletops and smaller containers, grown outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, fertile potting mix. Sparkles carries fine, dense white speckling scattered evenly across a deep green leaf surface rather than the broad central patch of cream seen on Camille or Compacta, giving the glossy, paddle-shaped foliage a flecked, glittering texture at close range. Its compact, densely-leaved habit stays smaller than standard dumb cane cultivars, making it a good fit for desks, shelves, and smaller pots. Water when the top inch of potting mix dries, keep it out of direct sun and cold drafts below 60°F, and wear gloves when pruning since the sap is irritating to skin and toxic if chewed by children or pets.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Dieffenbachia Species for Florida Interiors and Shade Gardens
